newsitem.title: USA: Martin Luther King's confessed killer gets hearing.
newsitem.headline: Martin Luther King's confessed killer gets hearing.

text.p: Conspiracy theories that have haunted the assassination of civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. for three decades may finally be aired in court on Thursday when a judge decides if James Earl Ray will get the trial his confession to the crime denied him.

Shelby County Criminal Court Judge Joe Brown set the one-day hearing to weigh claims from Ray's attorney that new scientific evidence will show that the rifle allegedly used in King's 1968 slaying was not the murder weapon.

The hearing will determine whether Ray, serving a 99-year sentence for the slaying, should finally receive the trial denied him because he confessed to the shooting -- a confession he recanted days later followed by a steady insistence on his innocence ever since.
Ray, 68, is dying of liver disease in a Nashville, Tennessee, prison hospital, and often confined to a wheelchair. He was not expected to attend the Memphis hearing.

The pressure for Ray to receive a trial increased last week when King's family, speaking out about the investigation for the first time, charged that the public had not been told the whole truth about the assassination.

"The lack of a satisfactory resolution to questions surrounding the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. has been a source of continuing pain and hardship to our family. Every effort must be made to determine the truth ... this can only be accomplished in a court of law," King's youngest son, Dexter King, told reporters in Atlanta.

British lawyer William Pepper, author of a 500-page book on the various theories about who killed King, will present Ray's plea over the dogged protests of prosecutors who insist the murder was solved and the conspiracy trails lead nowhere.

The death of the 39-year-old King, the soul and voice of the American civil rights movement, sparked urban riots and set off a drumbeat of conspiracy rumours similar to the unsubstantiated claims of a massive conspiracy that cling to the 1963 assassination of President John F. Kennedy.

Ray himself fuelled notions of a conspiracy by saying he bought the alleged murder weapon, a Remington hunting rifle, on orders from a mysterious man he could identify only as "Raoul" whom he had met earlier that year in a Montreal bar.

But a congressional committee that looked into the assassination in 1978 found that Ray had fired the single fatal shot into King's right cheek from the bathroom window of a shabby roominghouse overlooking the Lorraine Motel.

Pepper has said he would reveal Raoul's identity and whereabouts. But the Memphis Commercial Appeal newspaper recently said prosecutors had interviewed Raoul in New York City and found him completely innocent of any involvement.
